modifier.description:
Value type modifier

Non empty constraint is specified by adding an exclamation mark in front of the ValueType:
```type
  where: !Location
```

The desire to preserve empty values (such that they can be differentiated from the lack of any value) is specified
by adding a question mark in front of the ValueType:
```type
  approved: ?boolean
```

The non optional function parameter constraint is specified by adding `!?` in front of the ValueType:
```type
  f: function(url: !?string serialized Url)
```

@see #isNonEmpty
@see #preservesEmpty
@see #isNonOptionalParam
@see FunctionParam#isNonOptional

varBindings.description:
The map of variable bindings applied.

It is possible to have bind variable re-named. I.e. to have varBinding that itself is a variable of different name.

genericVars.description: The list of variable declarations and any restrictions on them.

params.description: The formal parameters accepted by this function.

returnType.description: The return type of the function.

stateful.description:
If this function is not a "pure" function of its arguments, it should be marked as such. A stateful function
return value cannot be cached. For example it is not valid to call it using HTTP GET. By default, it is assumed
all functions are pure (state and side-effect free).

title:
Value type for `lambda` i.e. function as a value. The structure of the lambda signature comes from
{@link FunctionType}. The implementation carried as data is what makes it a **lambda**.

Note that lambdas are _data values_ and thus a type field declared as a lambda is not defined by that type itself,
but will be a data field (with a {@link FieldType}). The field value may be null or may be supplied with a
lambda instance.

```type
type X {
  method: member function(a: !int): !int
  lambda: lambda(a: !int): !int
}
```

In the example above, **method** and **lambda** are both declared in the type, however, they are treated differently
because the first one is a {@link Method} and the second is a lambda. Instances of the Obj will have only a single
field, for **lambda**, and it will only be set if there is a value supplied. All instances will share the same
**method** and it will be implemented on the type itself.

```js
let x = X.make({ lambda: a => a * 2 })
x.method(3)
x.lambda(3)
```

```py
x = c3.X(lambda_ = lambda a: a * 2)
x.method(3)
x.lambda(3)
```

So in the above examples, both end up being callable from the instances, but the method implementation goes with
the type while the lambda implementation is a field value that goes with the instance.

```java
X x = X.builder().lambda(a -> a * 2).build();
x.method(3);
x.lambda().apply(3);
```

In Java, the lambdas are strongly typed (using the
[FunctionalInterface](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/FunctionalInterface.html) annotation),
so must be invoked using the correct method name. `apply` is appropriate here since this lambda will be a
[Function<Long, Long>](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/function/Function.html).

@see MethodType
@see methods.c3doc#lambdas
